narrative:
The model estimates you have a 32% chance of failing your final year, which is high enough that the school requires you to take remedial courses to strengthen your chances of graduating.

The prediction is driven mainly by three key aspects of your situation. The most influential factor is that you do not plan to pursue higher education. Among students who passed, every single one expressed a desire to continue studying after school; your lack of that intention strongly pulls the prediction toward failure. The second most important factor is your reason for choosing this school (wanting to stay close to home). This choice actually works in your favor and pushes the outcome slightly toward passing, because it is less common among students who ultimately fail. However, the third major influence—having already failed one class in the past—pulls the prediction back toward failing. While students who passed had zero previous failures on average, you have one, and the model sees this as a clear warning sign.

Taken together, the absence of higher-education goals and your prior failure outweigh the positive effect of your school-choice reason, leading to the decision that extra support is needed.

To improve, you should seriously reflect on your long-term goals and consider whether you might actually want to continue studying. Addressing any gaps from that past failure and building consistent study habits will also help turn the outlook around.
